paras: The attempted lynching of David Lewis took place near Elberton, Georgia, on 10 August 1881, when a crowd of Black people tried to take Lewis, a white man, from his guard after he killed a Black man named Governor Harper with a hoe. The guard fired small shot into the crowd and later dispersed it, and Lewis was afterward bound over to the Superior Court for involuntary manslaughter.

Lewis and Harper were among a number of men who had gathered to work the roads at the Goss place, two miles from Ruckersville. According to the Anderson Intelligencer, Lewis accused Harper of stealing fruit from Mrs. Goss, and one of Lewis's children said Harper's children had abused Lewis's cows; Harper denied both.

The argument grew heated, and the same account says Harper invited Lewis to fight and picked up a rock, at which Lewis struck him on the head with a hoe. The Elberton Gazette wrote that Harper 'died immediately', while the Anderson paper said he was struck about 9 a.m. and died about 1 p.m. despite the efforts of Dr. J. T. Heard.

Those present arrested Lewis, and while he was under guard 'a crowd of negroes attempted to lynch him'. One of the guard fired a double-barrelled gun into the crowd, 'peppering them with small shot', and the guard took Lewis to the house of a Mrs. Cleveland. The crowd followed to the gate and was finally dispersed, by threats from the guard in the Gazette's version and by an order from a 'Mr. John' in the Anderson account, whose text breaks off.

At a preliminary investigation in 'State vs. David Lewis', Lewis was found guilty of involuntary manslaughter and bound over in $200, and the bond 'was quickly found'. No report of an inquest, of any action against the crowd, or of the Superior Court's disposition of the case appears in the coverage.

The story reached other papers mainly through the Elberton Gazette, whose short paragraph ran in the Savannah Morning News's 'Georgia Affairs' column on 13 August and in the Marietta Journal's 'Georgia Gleanings' on 18 August. That version called Lewis 'Mr. David Lewis' and Harper 'a negro named Governor', and gave as much space to the guard's gunfire as to the killing. The Anderson Intelligencer in South Carolina printed a longer, separately written account the same day, naming both men by race and recording Harper's denials. The Savannah paper later carried the Gazette's note on the hearing, again among unrelated state items.
The accounts differ on when Harper died, immediately according to the Gazette or about four hours later according to the more detailed Anderson report, which also named the attending physician.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of David Lewis
bases: A crowd of Black people tried to take a white prisoner, David Lewis, from his guard to lynch him after he killed a Black man, Governor Harper; no one was killed by the crowd (A2, A3).

A 'crowd' attempted to take Lewis from his guard 'for the purpose of lynching him', but was driven off and he was not harmed (A2, A3); the papers do not state the crowd's reasons beyond the killing of Harper, and the targeted man was white.

The Elberton Gazette item (A2, reprinted in A4) and the separately worded Anderson Intelligencer account (A3) agree that Lewis killed Harper with a hoe and that a crowd of Black people tried to lynch Lewis while he was under guard.

accounts.label: Elberton Gazette (via Savannah Morning News)
accounts.gist: Lewis struck Governor with the eye of a hoe and he 'died immediately'; a crowd of negroes tried to lynch Lewis under guard, a guard fired small shot into them, and they were dispersed by threats at a nearby house.

accounts.label: Anderson Intelligencer
accounts.gist: A quarrel over stolen fruit and cows ended when Harper picked up a rock and Lewis hit him with a hoe; Harper died four hours later; a crowd of negroes tried to take Lewis to lynch him and followed the guard to Mrs. Cleveland's gate.

framing.detail: The Elberton Gazette paragraph, run in Savannah's 'Georgia Affairs' column, calls Lewis 'Mr. David Lewis' and Harper 'a negro named Governor', and describes the guard 'peppering' the crowd with small shot.
The Marietta Journal ran the same Gazette paragraph in its 'Georgia Gleanings' column.
The Anderson Intelligencer gave the fullest account, naming both men by race ('a white man', 'a colored man') and including Harper's denials and his picking up a rock.
